lessonRef.unitTitle: Drama, Media, and Point of View
lessonRef.title: Performance task planning: visual and audio rhetoric

studentTask.text: This Grade 7 lesson develops visual and audio rhetoric within the unit “Drama, Media, and Point of View.” Read the delivered Academy-original source before responding. Strong ELA work separates what the source explicitly says from what a reader infers, selects evidence because it is relevant and sufficient, and explains the connection instead of leaving a quotation to speak for itself. Today's performance task planning work asks you to make that reasoning visible and to revise if the evidence does not support the first idea.

sourceReference.text:
[1] At the small theater workshop, Mateo opened a folder containing a poem beside the prose paragraph that inspired it. A note on the cover read “Drama, Media, and Point of View,” but the pages inside told one unfinished story. Mateo expected the ending to explain everything. Instead, the first scene offered only a quiet choice: return a borrowed object without comment or admit why it had been kept.

[2] The main character rehearsed an apology three times. In the first version, every sentence began with “I.” In the second, the character blamed the confusing rules. In the third, the character named the harm, returned the object, and then stopped talking. The narrator never announced which version was sincere.

[3] Priya noticed that a repeated image—a door left slightly open—appeared before each rehearsal. At first it seemed like background description. By its third appearance, the image could suggest an invitation, an escape, or an unfinished decision. The story gave enough detail to support more than one interpretation but not enough to make every interpretation equally strong.

[4] The final scene ended before the apology was delivered. Mateo argued that the missing speech made the character seem afraid; Priya thought the pause showed care. To connect the scene to visual and audio rhetoric, each reader had to identify exact language, explain an inference, and account for the detail that made the other reading possible.

[5] Before revising, the group tested the source against the workshop goal: visual and audio rhetoric. They highlighted language that supported the goal, circled a detail that complicated it, and drew an arrow where the relationship between two ideas needed to be made explicit. The marks produced different possible readings, so the group had to defend priorities rather than copy a single approved answer.

guidedSupport.text:
Use this source-specific routine for “Reading Lab 119: visual and audio rhetoric”:
1. Preview the title and paragraph structure; write what visual and audio rhetoric asks you to notice or do.
2. Mark one statement the source makes explicitly and one inference a reader could draw. Keep the two kinds of thinking separate.
3. Test the inference with the evidence requirement in today's task. If the evidence is weak or incomplete, narrow or revise the inference.
4. Draft your own response. A facilitator may clarify directions or ask questions, but may not supply your claim, evidence choice, sentences, or revision.

independentEvidenceTask.text:
Read “Reading Lab 119: visual and audio rhetoric,” then answer: Plan a response about visual and audio rhetoric. Which claim, evidence sequence, and ending will make the plan coherent?

Deliverable: Grade 7: a complete writing plan naming the claim or controlling idea, evidence order, and ending move; write three or four developed paragraphs.

Evidence requirement: Use two well-chosen details with paragraph numbers. Label source evidence with a paragraph number or another precise location. Your response must explain the connection between the evidence and your conclusion.

remediation.text:
If visual and audio rhetoric is not yet secure, return to “Reading Lab 119: visual and audio rhetoric” before starting over:
- Evidence gap: underline the exact words that support the idea and label their paragraph or location.
- Reasoning gap: complete the stem “This evidence matters because …” in your own words, then reread the question.
- Overclaim: name what the source does not establish and narrow the conclusion to what the evidence can support.
- Completion gap: compare the draft with each learner success criterion and repair one missing part at a time.

extension.text: Apply visual and audio rhetoric to a different paragraph or a defensible alternative interpretation of “Reading Lab 119: visual and audio rhetoric.” Compare the new result with your first response and explain which evidence changes, which reasoning still holds, and why.
